explanations.explanation: That's the one, baker. He says, "I am He; I am the first, and I am the last." (Isaiah 48:12) Nobody got here before Him, and nobody is coming after. When somebody opens with that, I don't ask for a business card.

explanations.answer: A god of the high hills
explanations.explanation: I see why that one looks tempting, baker, but the text never says it. The LORD says, "I am He; I am the first, and I am the last." (Isaiah 48:12) No hills, no height, no mountain address. He just says who He is, and He starts with the very first and the very last.

Not quite, friend. He says, "I am He; I am the first, and I am the last." (Isaiah 48:12) You can't be the first and the last and also fit in a lineup. Right after this, He asks which of the idols has foretold these things (Isaiah 48:14), and I think that tells you how He sees the lineup.
Yes, baker. "When I summon them, they stand up together." (Isaiah 48:13) The earth and the heavens show up as one. No late ones, no stragglers, and no one hitting snooze.

That's a rough picture, friend, and it isn't in the verse. The text says, "when I summon them, they stand up together." (Isaiah 48:13) Nothing shakes and nothing crumbles. Think of a batch of cookies that all come out of the oven perfect, with no broken ones.

Nope, nobody's ducking behind the couch here. The verse says, "when I summon them, they stand up together." (Isaiah 48:13) When He calls, they stand up. I think I'd have tried to hide, but I'm no heaven.
Close, baker, but this one is False. The LORD asks, "Which of the idols has foretold these things?" (Isaiah 48:14) It's a question, and the idols don't answer it. All that silence says plenty.
That's right, baker. The LORD asks, "Which of the idols has foretold these things?" (Isaiah 48:14) He asks it and no idol steps up. I'd call that the quietest room in the whole passage.

That's it, baker. "The LORD's chosen ally will carry out His desire against Babylon, and His arm will be against the Chaldeans." (Isaiah 48:14) The Chaldeans are mentioned right alongside it. Both names will come back when we hit verse 20.

Good guess, since Nineveh was a big name in the Bible. But it's not here, friend. The verse says the chosen ally will act "against Babylon, and His arm will be against the Chaldeans." (Isaiah 48:14) Wrong city, right neighborhood of big ancient names.

Damascus is a real city in the Bible, baker, but it isn't named here. The text says the LORD's chosen ally will carry out His desire "against Babylon, and His arm will be against the Chaldeans." (Isaiah 48:14) When you're stuck, the verse itself is the best map I know.
Yes, baker. "I have brought him, and he will succeed in his mission." (Isaiah 48:15) That's a promise, not a hope. When the LORD brings someone, the job gets done.
I know, friend, it sounds like how my Monday goes. But the verse says, "I have brought him, and he will succeed in his mission." (Isaiah 48:15) No struggling is mentioned here. Only success.

Not this time, baker. The LORD says, "I have brought him, and he will succeed in his mission." (Isaiah 48:15) Nobody's standing at the door with cold feet. The text says he succeeds, and that's all it says.
Good thought, baker, but it's False. The LORD says, "From the beginning I have not spoken in secret." (Isaiah 48:16) He's been out in the open this whole time. No whispering behind the cooling racks.
That's right, baker. "From the beginning I have not spoken in secret." (Isaiah 48:16) He says it plainly, in the open. Nothing is hidden in the back of a drawer.

Yes, baker. "And now the Lord GOD has sent me, accompanied by His Spirit." (Isaiah 48:16) The verse doesn't tell us who this speaker is, and I won't guess. What it does say is clear: the Lord GOD sent him, and His Spirit comes along.

Whoa, wrong palace, friend. The speaker says, "the Lord GOD has sent me, accompanied by His Spirit." (Isaiah 48:16) Babylon is the place the LORD's chosen ally acts against in verse 14. A king from there sending him wouldn't fit.

I get why you'd look there, baker, but the elders aren't mentioned in this passage. The speaker says, "the Lord GOD has sent me, accompanied by His Spirit." (Isaiah 48:16) The sender is right there in the verse. No committee needed.

explanations.answer: Directs them in the way to go
explanations.explanation: That's it, baker. The LORD says He is the One "who directs you in the way you should go." (Isaiah 48:17) He teaches and He directs. So He's not only handing out lessons, He's pointing at the road too.

explanations.answer: Lets them pick their own road
explanations.explanation: Not quite, friend. The LORD says He "directs you in the way you should go." (Isaiah 48:17) He doesn't hand over the keys and say good luck. He points the way.
That's not what He says, baker. He is the One "who directs you in the way you should go." (Isaiah 48:17) A hidden road can't be directed. He says He directs it.
Yes, baker, peace goes in the first blank. "Your peace would have been like a river." (Isaiah 48:18) A river keeps on coming, wave after wave. That's what He says they could have had.
That's right, baker. "And your righteousness like waves of the sea." (Isaiah 48:18) Waves keep rolling in and never run out. Two big pictures, one if only.

Nice try, friend, but money never comes up here. The LORD says their peace would have been like a river, "and your righteousness like waves of the sea." (Isaiah 48:18) Peace and righteousness are what He names.

Good thinking, but a harvest isn't in this verse, baker. The LORD says "your peace would have been like a river, and your righteousness like waves of the sea." (Isaiah 48:18) The pictures here are water, not crops.
Not this time, friend. The verse has no armies at all. It says "your peace would have been like a river, and your righteousness like waves of the sea." (Isaiah 48:18)

Right, baker. "Your descendants would have been as countless as the sand, and your offspring as numerous as its grains." (Isaiah 48:19) That's more descendants than I have crumbs on my counter after a big batch. It's still the same if only, though.

Careful, friend, this one is True. The LORD says, "Your descendants would have been as countless as the sand." (Isaiah 48:19) He even adds that their offspring would be as numerous as its grains. That's a whole lot of sand.

Yes, baker. "Their name would never be cut off or eliminated from My presence." (Isaiah 48:19) A name matters, and He says theirs would never be erased from His presence. That's the picture of the if only.
Good guess, friend, but land isn't what this verse says. It says "their name would never be cut off or eliminated from My presence." (Isaiah 48:19) The word is name.
Not quite, baker. The temple isn't mentioned in this verse. The LORD says "their name would never be cut off or eliminated from My presence." (Isaiah 48:19)
That's right, baker. "Leave Babylon! Flee from the Chaldeans! Declare it with a shout of joy." (Isaiah 48:20) The leaving comes with a shout of joy. They don't sneak out, they announce it.
Close, friend, but it's True. Right after "Flee from the Chaldeans!" the verse says, "Declare it with a shout of joy." (Isaiah 48:20) It's a call to be loud about it.
Yes, baker. "The LORD has redeemed His servant Jacob!" (Isaiah 48:20) That's the news that goes out to the ends of the earth. Good news travels faster than a smell of fresh cookies.
That's right, baker. "The LORD has redeemed His servant Jacob!" (Isaiah 48:20) Jacob is the name the LORD uses for His people in this passage (Isaiah 48:12). He calls him His servant.

No, friend, that's the opposite of the news. The message is, "The LORD has redeemed His servant Jacob!" (Isaiah 48:20) Redeemed, not forgotten. I know a thing or two about the other word, and this isn't it.
Not this one, baker. The shout going out is, "The LORD has redeemed His servant Jacob!" (Isaiah 48:20) That's the word that fits a shout of joy.
Moses was Israel's leader, so I see why he came to mind. But the shout names someone else: "The LORD has redeemed His servant Jacob!" (Isaiah 48:20) Right story neighborhood, different name.
Not quite, baker, this one is False. The verse says, "They did not thirst when He led them through the deserts." (Isaiah 48:21) They went through the desert and still weren't thirsty.
That's right, baker. "They did not thirst when He led them through the deserts." (Isaiah 48:21) Desert, yes. Thirst, no. He led, and they weren't thirsty.
Yes, baker. "There is no peace," says the LORD, "for the wicked." (Isaiah 48:22) It's a short line and a heavy one. After a river of peace in verse 18, this is a quiet stop.
No, friend, the poor aren't named here. The LORD says, "There is no peace," "for the wicked." (Isaiah 48:22) The word is wicked.
I understand the guess, baker, because the weary sure could use peace. But the verse says, "There is no peace," says the LORD, "for the wicked." (Isaiah 48:22) The weary aren't named there.
